rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mursalāt is an early Makkan sūra.
rows.anchor: some early commentators, such as Ibn ʿAbbās

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Qatādah
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Qatādah maintain that verse 48 is Madinan.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Qatādah, maintain that v. 48 is Madinan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra takes its name from the mention of those sent forth in its first verse.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the mention of those sent forth in the first verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also called al-ʿUrf after the second word of verse 1, ʿurfan, meaning in succession.
rows.anchor: al-ʿUrf after the second word in the first verse, ʿurfan (Āl), which can mean in succession

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith reports that the sūra was revealed in a cave; the Prophet ordered a snake killed, then said it and the Companions had escaped each other's evil.
rows.anchor: Suddenly a snake came out, and the Messenger of God said, ‘Get it and kill it!’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening oaths and reminders of the Last Day lead into signs of that Day and the refrain first appearing at verse 15.
rows.anchor: After a series of oaths and reminders of the Last Day (vv.1–6) and descriptions of its signs (vv. 8–14)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Woe that Day to the deniers recurs ten times as the sūra's refrain.
rows.anchor: which thereafter serves as a refrain repeated ten times in the sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra says guilty people of every generation meet the same end, then presents gestation and the created order as signs of God's Power, and the earth as a sign of Power and Mercy.
rows.anchor: The sūrah then affirms that the guilty of all generations will meet the same end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning directs deniers toward the punishment they denied, then contrasts it with the rewards of the reverent and virtuous.
rows.anchor: It then addresses the disbelievers, ordering them toward that which they deny and warning them of the punishments such denial entails

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion addresses disbelievers and criticizes their failure to pray and believe.
rows.anchor: The sūrah concludes with a final address to the disbelievers and criticism of their failure to pray and to believe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human creation from a base fluid recalls humble origins and testifies to God's creative power and ability to resurrect people.
rows.anchor: The creation of the human being from a base fluid (cf. 32:8) is cited in several verses to remind people of their humble origins

rows.speaker: IK and Ṭ
rows.claim: IK and Ṭ identify the secure dwelling place as the womb.
rows.anchor: The secure dwelling place is a reference to the womb (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The known measure refers to the phases of gestation described at 22:5 and 23:14.
rows.anchor: a known measure refers to the phases of gestation outlined in 22:5 and 23:14

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fail to recognize their own creation deny God and become manifest adversaries to God and themselves.
rows.anchor: those who do not recognize the nature of their own creation deny God and are thus a manifest adversary (16:4; 36:77)

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: Sh reads the third warning at verse 24 with verse 23, as a warning about how God determines.
rows.anchor: This third occurrence of Woe that Day in v. 24 can be read in connection with v. 23 and thus as a warning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell is where those who rebel against the truth are sent.
rows.anchor: Hell is the place to which those who rebel against the truth are sent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell ambushes them at death because they were oblivious to the truth in worldly life.
rows.anchor: It will come upon them like an ambush when they die, because they had been oblivious to the truth in this world

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads rebellion as corruption of intellect: those who know God recognize their insignificance and do not incline toward arrogance.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī interprets one who rebels to indicate corruption of the intellect, for all who know God know their own insignificance

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads preferring worldly life as corruption in action.
rows.anchor: Prefers the life of this world is then taken to indicate corruption in actions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary cites a hadith saying love of the world is the source of all error.
rows.anchor: The love of the world is the source of all error

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Together, intellectual and practical corruption represent the greatest corruption and merit eternal punishment; Hell is the refuge for those reaching this level.
rows.anchor: The two together are thus taken to indicate the greatest degree of corruption, the punishment for which is eternal

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Those who do not reach this level may still be punished, but Hell will not be their ultimate refuge.
rows.anchor: Those who do not may still be punished, but Hellfire will not be their ultimate refuge (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses condemn preferring worldly life: it is delusive enjoyment, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring.
rows.anchor: Many verses condemn those who prefer the life of this world over the life of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is admonished for turning from a guidance seeker toward people he hoped to attract to Islam.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is here admonished for turning away from one who sought guidance to others whom he hoped to attract to Islam

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet could not make people accept religion; his role was to convey God's message and guide those who accepted it.
rows.anchor: he was not responsible for making people accept religion, only for conveying God’s message and guiding those who accepted it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses instruct the Prophet to be patient and not turn away from people seeking religion.
rows.anchor: Other verses tell the Prophet to be patient and to not turn away from those who seek religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istaghna literally means self-sufficient and connotes seeing oneself as self-sufficient in relation to God.
rows.anchor: Beyond need (v. 5) translates man istaghnā, which literally means

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fear in verse 9 is fear of God and the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: The fear mentioned in v. 9 is fear of God and the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Safarah can refer to attendant angels who inscribe servants' deeds in books.
rows.anchor: a reference to the attendant angels who “inscribe”

rows.speaker: Q and Ṭ
rows.claim: Safarah can refer to angels appointed as mediators between God and His messengers.
rows.anchor: angels whom God has appointed as “mediators”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A famous hadith says that a proficient Quran reciter who has memorized it is with the noble, pious scribes.
rows.anchor: A famous ḥadīth states, “One who recites the Quran proficiently and has memorized it is with the scribes, noble and pious” (IK)

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some argue that scribes here should mean mediators, since human beings can mediate God's message to one another.
rows.anchor: Some argue that here scribes should be “mediators” to indicate the function of mediating God’s message

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Safara can mean unveil, alluding to the Quran's clarification of matters.
rows.anchor: Safara can also mean “to unveil”; thus some take it as an allusion to the Quran’s making matters clear

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others take the hands of scribes to refer to Quran reciters.
rows.anchor: Others say that the hands of scribes refers to the reciters of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qutila al-insan means may man perish.
rows.anchor: May man perish translates qutila al-insān

rows.speaker: IK and Q
rows.claim: IK and Q also render the phrase as may man be cursed.
rows.anchor: could also be rendered, “May man be cursed” (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The phrase refers to deniers without an argument, who lack knowledge of the truth and think it far-fetched.
rows.anchor: refer to those who deny the truth without any supporting argument, but only because they lack knowledge of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afkara indicates both ingratitude toward God and disbelief in God.
rows.anchor: Ungrateful translates afkara, which indicates both ingratitude toward and disbelief in God

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q records readings that man is accursed for what he disbelieves, or asks what mankind disbelieves.
rows.anchor: Thus this verse could also be read, “Man is accursed for what he disbelieves,” or “Mankind is accursed; for what does he disbelieve?” (Q)

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say the verse concerns an individual who accepted Islam then apostatized when Sūrah 53 was revealed, and was cursed for rejecting the Quran after believing.
rows.anchor: According to some, this verse relates to a specific individual who had accepted Islam, but apostatized when Sūrah 53 was revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation of the human from a drop is evidence of God's Omnipotence, as in other passages.
rows.anchor: This is one of several passages in which the creation of the human being from a drop is cited as evidence of God’s Omnipotence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two deluders are worldly life and Satan, called the Deluder.
rows.anchor: Two things are said to delude human beings, the life of this world and Satan, the Deluder

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Fashioning refers to making human parts and faculties sound and functional.
rows.anchor: Fashioned you refers to the manner in which God has made all human parts and faculties sound and functional

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text's ʿaddalaka can also be read ʿadalaka, turned, meaning God can turn people in any direction; both readings work, but ʿaddalaka is grammatically better if verse 8 continues verse 7.
rows.anchor: meaning “turned you,” implying that God turns people in any direction

words: فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ
rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some understand the verse as God choosing a particular human form for each person.
rows.anchor: Some take this verse to indicate the manner in which God chooses a particular human form for each individual

words: فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ
rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others understand that God can assemble humans in the form of other animals, presumably as punishment, as in the transformation of the people addressed at 2:65.
rows.anchor: Others take this to mean that God can assemble human beings in the form of other animals

rows.speaker: Qu and R
rows.claim: Verses 7–8 can refer to inner qualities, such as states of faith or disobedience, rather than outer form.
rows.anchor: Vv. 7–8 can also be taken to imply the inner qualities rather than the outer form, thus referring to states of faith or disobedience

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses can also refer to states of felicity or wretchedness, commonly understood as salvation and damnation.
rows.anchor: which are commonly understood as referring to states of damnation and salvation

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators agree that Tasnīm is Heaven's purest and noblest drink.
rows.anchor: Most commentators agree that Tasnīm is the purest and noblest drink of Heaven

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say Tasnīm flows from the Divine Throne into Paradise.
rows.anchor: Some say that it flows from the Divine Throne into Paradise

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some understand Tasnīm as a proper name with no specific meaning.
rows.anchor: Tasnīm is understood by some as a proper name with no specific meaning

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others derive Tasnīm from sannama, to raise, so it raises or ennobles drinkers.
rows.anchor: Others propose that it derives from the verb sannama, “to raise,” indicating that it raises or ennobles those who drink it

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Tasnīm is alluded to at 32:17.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn ʿAbbās, Tasnīm is what is alluded to in 32:17

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say Tasnīm is a spring mixed with the pure sealed wine for the companions of the right, while those brought near drink its purest form.
rows.anchor: Some say that Tasnīm is a spring whose waters are mixed with the pure wine sealed for the companions of the right

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others say those brought near drink Tasnīm unmixed, while all other inhabitants of Paradise drink it mixed.
rows.anchor: Similarly, others say those brought nigh drink of it unmixed, while all the other inhabitants of Paradise drink of it mixed

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī reads Tasnīm as knowledge of God and delight in gazing upon Him: the brought-near see only God, while companions of the right also attend to created paradisal delights, hence their mixed drink.
rows.anchor: According to al-Rāzī, Tasnīm “is the knowledge of God

rows.speaker: Some Sufi commentators
rows.claim: Some Sufi commentators identify Tasnīm with the highest level of spiritual love.
rows.anchor: Some Sufi commentators have identified Tasnīm with the highest level of spiritual love

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says every deed, good or bad, will be met with God.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn ʿAbbās, this verse means, “Whatever deed you do, you will meet God with it, whether it is good or bad”

rows.speaker: Maybudī
rows.claim: Maybudī understands the verse as urging mindfulness because every moment brings one closer to God.
rows.anchor: Maybudī understands it as an injunction to be mindful, since every moment is a step closer to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joy among his people signifies worldly life and the heedlessness of disbelievers who rejected return to God and the Resurrection reckoning.
rows.anchor: Among his people he was joyful refers to the life of this world; it represents the heedlessness of those who did not believe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says the world is the believer's prison and the disbeliever's garden.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth says, “The world is the prison of the believer and the garden of the disbeliever”

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Nay means they will in fact return; God has observed all their actions from creation until resurrection.
rows.anchor: God has been aware of all their actions from the moment He created them until the moment He resurrects them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is another sign of God: those who fail to read created signs should recognize the Quran's miracle and its signs.
rows.anchor: Here the Quran is invoked as another sign of God, as if to say, “If they cannot read the signs of God in the created world

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some take prostrating to mean prayer.

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others take prostrating to mean humility.
rows.anchor: Others say it refers to humility

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators count this among fifteen verses after which one prostrates when reciting the Quran.
rows.anchor: Most maintain that this is one of fifteen verses after which one prostrates when reciting the Quran

rows.speaker: Imam Mālik and other Mālikī jurists
rows.claim: Imam Mālik does not require prostration after this verse, while other Mālikī jurists do.
rows.anchor: Imam Mālik does not maintain that one is obligated to prostrate after reciting this verse, but other Mālikī jurists do

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭāriq is an early Makkan sūra, most likely revealed after Sūrah 90, al-Balad.
rows.anchor: n early Makkan sūrah, al-Ṭāriq was most likely revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra's title is al-Ṭāriq, from its first verse and the verb ṭaraqa, meaning to pound.
rows.anchor: a word that derives from the verbṭaraqa, meaning “to pound.”

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some understand al-Ṭāriq as the way, since feet pound the path as they walk.
rows.anchor: understood by some to indicate “the way,” because the path is pounded by the feet that walk upon it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭāriq can mean that which comes by night or the night visitant, since night arrivals pound on closed doors to gain entry.
rows.anchor: Since doors are closed at night, when people arrive at this time, they must pound on them to gain entry

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some understand al-Ṭāriq as a reference to the Morning Star.
rows.anchor: Al-ṭariq is also understood by some as a reference to the Morning Star

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra opens with an oath on heaven and celestial bodies, reflects on the soul, humble physical origins, and return to God, then gives an echoing oath and a final warning.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with an oath by Heaven and the celestial bodies (vv. 1–3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is reported that the Prophet often recited this and the preceding sūra as part of the two afternoon prayers.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet would often recite this and the previous sūrah as part of the two afternoon prayers

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Those who deny resurrection should reflect on how God created them.
rows.anchor: Let those who deny the Resurrection reflect upon the manner in which God created them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse can also call people to recognize their purpose in creation, as in the call to worship at 51:56.
rows.anchor: This verse can also be understood as a call to recognize that for which the human being was created

rows.speaker: Maybudī
rows.claim: Maybudī describes humans as created for prostration, heed, service, knowledge, and love, with tongues adorned by testimony, hearts by knowledge and joy, and bodies by worship.
rows.anchor: God created a face fit for prostration, eyes fit for taking heed, a body fit for service, a heart fit for knowledge

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some understand the loins and pelvic arch as the man's and woman's respective parts, whose sperm and egg form the fetus.
rows.anchor: are understood by some to refer to the respective parts of the man and the woman, whose sperm and egg form the fetus

rows.speaker: Others
rows.claim: Others restrict the loins and pelvic arch to the male and identify them as the area from which his fluid gushes.
rows.anchor: others restrict them to the male (Ṭ, Ṭs), saying that loins and pelvic arch refer to the area from which a man’s fluid gushes
